fields.title: The Illusion of Safety
fields.description: Test your understanding of this AI failure case study

fields.prompt: The Rivertown dashboard was criticised for 'False Precision.' Which specific design choice created this illusion?

fields.text: The map used low-resolution satellite imagery that was hard to read.
The developers used a sharp, binary line to separate 'Safe' from 'Unsafe' instead of showing uncertainty.
The system displayed too many decimal places in the flood depth predictions.

fields.prompt: The AI model suffered from the 'Stationarity Assumption.' What does this mean in the context of the failure?

fields.text: It assumed the river water would remain stationary (not move).
It assumed that future rainfall patterns would look exactly like the last 50 years of history.
It assumed that the population of Rivertown would not grow.

fields.prompt: Why did 90% of the flooded residents fail to purchase flood insurance?

fields.text: The insurance website was down during the storm.
The 'Official Safe Zone' label on the authoritative map led them to believe they had zero risk.
The cost of insurance was too high for the area.

fields.prompt: Which organisational failure contributed to the disaster?

fields.text: The developers used Python instead of C++.
There was no 'Human-in-the-Loop' to manually review the edge cases near the flood walls.
The servers were not powerful enough to run the model in real-time.

fields.prompt: If you were redesigning this system today, how would you visualise the risk to be more responsible?

fields.text: I would use a colour gradient (fading from green to red) to indicate areas where the model is unsure.
I would make the blue line thicker so it is easier to see.
I would hide the map entirely and only show text alerts.

fields.title: Beyond the Blue Line
fields.description: Test your understanding of this AI failure case study

fields.prompt: The storm that caused the flooding was described as a '1-in-100-year' event. What does this case reveal about using historical frequency to predict future risk?

fields.text: 1-in-100-year events only happen once per century, so the model was unlucky.

Climate change is increasing the frequency of extreme weather events, a '1-in-100-year' storm based on historical data may now occur far more often, making the model's risk assessment dangerously outdated.
The storm was so unusual that no model could have predicted it.

fields.prompt: The model assumed flood walls would perform perfectly. Why is this assumption dangerous?

fields.text: Flood walls are always maintained to a perfect standard.

Physical infrastructure degrades over time, cracks, maintenance failures, and material fatigue can cause flood walls to leak or fail during extreme events, and the model had no way to account for this.
Flood walls are not relevant to flood risk.

fields.prompt: The dashboard displayed risk on a 4K interactive map with high-resolution LiDAR data. How did this visual quality contribute to the failure?

fields.text: Higher resolution maps are always more accurate.
The visual sharpness and detail created an impression of precision and reliability, users assumed that because the map looked authoritative, the underlying predictions must be equally precise.
4K resolution slowed down the system and caused delays.

fields.prompt: The failure was not detected by any audit or monitoring system. It was discovered by residents during the flood. What does this reveal about the oversight process?

fields.text: Audits are always effective at catching model failures.

The oversight process did not include stress-testing the model against scenarios beyond its training data, no one asked 'what happens if the storm exceeds anything in the historical record?' until it actually did.
The residents should have reported concerns earlier.

fields.prompt: 500 families were flooded and 90% had no insurance. Who bears the primary responsibility?

fields.text: The residents, for not buying insurance despite living near a river.
The council and the system's developers, for deploying a tool that presented unverified predictions as certainties and for removing the human oversight that might have caught the error.
The weather service, for not predicting the storm accurately.

fields.title: The Wrong Forest
fields.description: Test your understanding of this AI failure case study

fields.prompt: Why did the AI rate the Portuguese scrubland as 'Low Risk' on the morning of the fire?

fields.text: The satellite imagery was corrupted by cloud cover.
The model interpreted sparse, low vegetation as low fuel, but Mediterranean scrub burns fast and hot.
The fire was started by arson, which no AI can predict.

fields.prompt: What critical step was skipped before deploying the system in Southern Europe?

fields.text: The developers forgot to install the software on local servers.
Local calibration and validation against Mediterranean fire history.
The fire service didn't purchase the premium version of the software.

fields.prompt: The model treated recent rainfall as a strong protective factor. Why was this wrong for the Mediterranean?

fields.text: Mediterranean rain is too warm to reduce fire risk.
Mediterranean summers can go months without rain, the model's assumption that summer rainfall is common was borrowed from temperate climates and didn't apply.
The rain sensors were not installed in Portugal.

fields.prompt: Fire crews were sent 80 km north based on the model's prediction. What does this reveal about the real-world consequences of model error?

fields.text: The crews were needed in both locations simultaneously.
A false prediction doesn't just fail to warn, it actively misdirects resources, making the real emergency worse by pulling responders away from where they were actually needed.
80 km is not a significant distance for fire services.

fields.prompt: The system had no mechanism for fire commanders to flag false predictions. Why is this a critical design flaw?

fields.text: Fire commanders are not qualified to evaluate AI predictions.
Without a feedback loop, the model cannot learn from its mistakes, the same false prediction can repeat daily because no one can correct it. Local expertise is locked out of the system.
Feedback would slow down the prediction process.

fields.title: The Universal Tool That Wasn't
fields.description: Test your understanding of this AI failure case study

fields.prompt: The system was marketed as a 'universal' wildfire tool. What is dangerous about this claim?

fields.text: Marketing claims should not use the word 'universal.'
'Universal' implies the tool works everywhere, discouraging buyers from asking whether it was tested in their specific environment, the marketing claim substituted for local validation.
The tool was universal but needed a software update.

fields.prompt: The model achieved 94% accuracy in Northern France and Germany. Why was this figure irrelevant for Portugal?

fields.text: 94% is not high enough for safety-critical applications.
Accuracy measured in temperate forests tells you nothing about performance in Mediterranean scrubland, the 94% was valid only for the conditions it was tested in, which were fundamentally different.
The accuracy was measured using a different metric in Portugal.

fields.prompt: The AI interpreted 'low vegetation density' as 'low fuel load.' What is the correct interpretation for Mediterranean scrubland?

fields.text: Low vegetation density always means low fire risk.
Mediterranean scrub is low and sparse but composed of oily, highly flammable plants, low density means fast-spreading ground fire, not low risk.
Scrubland cannot catch fire because it is too close to the ground.

fields.prompt: 14 people were hospitalised and three villages evacuated. How should the human cost factor into decisions about deploying predictive models?

fields.text: Human cost is unrelated to model deployment decisions.

The potential consequences of model failure must be weighed against the convenience of deployment, in safety-critical applications, the cost of a wrong prediction (hospitalisation, evacuation, death) must drive the rigour of testing and validation.
14 hospitalisations is a statistically acceptable error rate.

fields.prompt: If the Southern European Forestry Commission had followed best practices, what should they have done before deploying the system?

fields.text: Asked the vendor for a discount.

Conducted a local validation study using Mediterranean fire history, recalibrated the model's thresholds for local vegetation and climate, run a parallel trial alongside existing methods, and established a feedback mechanism for field commanders.
Installed more weather stations across the region.

fields.title: The Missing Season
fields.description: Test your understanding of this AI failure case study

fields.prompt: Why did the AI's accuracy drop so dramatically in autumn and winter?

fields.text: The drones flew at a different altitude in winter, making images blurry.
The training data was almost entirely from spring and summer, so the model had never learned what plants look like in their dormant state.
Invasive willow only grows during winter months.

fields.prompt: How was the failure eventually discovered?

fields.text: The AI flagged its own declining accuracy and sent an alert.
A routine annual field visit by ecologists revealed the invasive spread.
Satellite imagery from a different agency contradicted the AI's reports.

fields.prompt: The AI's confidence scores dropped significantly in winter, but this wasn't noticed. Why?

fields.text: Confidence scores were not recorded during winter.
The scores were averaged into summary statistics that masked the seasonal decline, individual low-confidence classifications were hidden inside overall averages.
The confidence scores were only visible to the AI developer.

fields.prompt: The model treated each image as an independent snapshot. What capability would have helped detect the invasive spread?

fields.text: Higher resolution cameras.
Change detection, the ability to compare images of the same area over time and flag locations where vegetation is spreading or changing in patterns consistent with invasive species.
More frequent drone flights.

fields.prompt: The remediation cost was $2.1 million NZD. How does this compare to the cost of collecting winter training data?

fields.text: Winter training data would have been equally expensive.
Collecting a winter training dataset would have cost a fraction of the remediation, the cost of proper data collection is almost always far less than the cost of a failure caused by inadequate data.
The remediation cost is unrelated to the training data gap.

fields.title: The Automated Ecologist
fields.description: Test your understanding of this AI failure case study

fields.prompt: The agency replaced monthly field visits with weekly AI reports. What principle did this violate?

fields.text: The principle that AI should never be used in conservation.
The principle that AI should augment human expertise, not replace it, removing field visits eliminated the only independent verification of the AI's outputs.
The principle that weekly reports are less useful than monthly visits.

fields.prompt: The system achieved 91% accuracy in summer pilot testing. Why was this an insufficient basis for full deployment?

fields.text: 91% is not high enough for any application.

The 91% was measured only in summer conditions, it told the agency nothing about performance in autumn, winter, or adverse weather. Deploying based on single-season testing left half the year untested.
Pilot testing is never reliable.

fields.prompt: Invasive willow spread across 30% of the restoration area over four months. Why is this particularly difficult to reverse?

fields.text: Willow trees are protected by New Zealand law.
Invasive species establish root systems, disperse seeds, and alter soil conditions, four months of unchecked spread creates years of remediation work, and some ecological damage may be permanent.
The restoration area was too large to manage manually.

fields.prompt: What minimum standard should apply to training data for environmental monitoring systems?

fields.text: Data from the most common season is sufficient if accuracy is above 90%.

Training data must cover all seasons, weather conditions, and environmental states the system will encounter, with explicit documentation of any gaps and corresponding limitations on the model's deployment scope.
Training data should be as large as possible regardless of seasonal coverage.

fields.prompt: If you were redesigning this system, what would be the single most important change?

fields.text: Use a more powerful neural network architecture.
Build an automatic confidence monitoring system that alerts ecologists when the model's average confidence drops below a threshold, triggering a mandatory field visit to verify the AI's outputs.
Fly the drones more frequently.

fields.title: The Uneven Standard
fields.description: Test your understanding of this AI failure case study

fields.prompt: What was the core data problem that caused the app to fail on darker skin tones?

fields.text: Camera quality on phones in Nigeria was lower.
Fewer than 5% of training images depicted medium-to-dark skin types, so the model had almost no examples to learn from.
Melanoma is a different disease on darker skin and cannot be detected by AI.

fields.prompt: Why was the app's published accuracy of 95% misleading?

fields.text: The researchers fabricated their results.
The 95% was only achieved on the population tested (mostly lighter skin), with no subgroup analysis published before launch.
The accuracy was measured on training data, not test data.

fields.prompt: Why is a 'Low Risk' result from a poorly validated tool more dangerous than no result at all?

fields.text: It isn't, any information is better than none.
A false 'Low Risk' result actively delays the user from seeking medical attention, creating a window where the cancer can progress, the tool caused harm by providing false reassurance.
Users ignore 'Low Risk' results anyway.

fields.prompt: The app gave the same confident percentage score to every user regardless of how well it performed on their skin type. What should it have done instead?

fields.text: Refused to work on darker skin tones.

Asked users to indicate their skin type, displayed a warning when performance was likely to be reduced, and recommended professional consultation when the model's confidence was low for the input characteristics.
Only displayed results for light-skinned users.

fields.prompt: The disparity was discovered by an independent academic study, not by the company. What does this suggest about AI healthcare governance?

fields.text: Companies should conduct their own evaluations exclusively.
Independent, third-party evaluation across diverse populations should be required before health AI tools launch, companies have insufficient incentive to discover their own products' failures.
Academic studies are unreliable.

fields.title: Designing for Everyone
fields.description: Test your understanding of this AI failure case study

fields.prompt: The app was downloaded 2 million times globally. What responsibility comes with global reach?

fields.text: None, users download at their own risk.

Global deployment requires global validation. If the app is available in countries with predominantly dark-skinned populations, it must be validated for those populations, otherwise it is marketing a product it knows (or should know) is unsafe for many users.
The app should only be available in countries where it was tested.

fields.prompt: What change to the original clinical trial would have caught this problem before launch?

fields.text: Running a larger trial with more participants.

Stratifying the trial by Fitzpatrick skin type and reporting sensitivity and specificity separately for each group, ensuring the published results reflected performance for all users, not just the average.
Conducting the trial at multiple hospitals in the same country.

fields.prompt: Three patients presented with more advanced melanoma after being reassured by the app. What does this tell us about the real-world stakes of AI accuracy claims?

fields.text: Three cases is too small a number to be significant.

Each percentage point of missed sensitivity in a cancer screening tool represents real people whose diagnosis is delayed, and delayed melanoma diagnosis can mean the difference between a minor procedure and life-threatening disease.
The patients should not have relied solely on the app.

fields.prompt: The training data was 95% light skin. Whose responsibility is it to ensure diverse training data?

fields.text: The hospitals that contributed the images.
The company developing the product, they chose to build a global health tool and had the responsibility to ensure their training data represented the global population they intended to serve.
Data diversity is a nice-to-have, not a requirement.

fields.prompt: What regulatory measure would most effectively prevent similar failures in health AI apps?

fields.text: Ban all AI-based health apps.

Require pre-market evaluation across all major demographic subgroups, mandate disclosure of performance by demographic in the app's interface, and conduct post-market surveillance with mandatory adverse event reporting.
Require apps to include a disclaimer that results may vary.

fields.title: Trust Your Instinct
fields.description: Test your understanding of this AI failure case study

fields.prompt: Why did the chatbot consistently under-triage younger patients with cardiac symptoms?

fields.text: The chatbot was not programmed to ask about chest pain.
The model over-weighted age as a protective factor, treating younger patients as inherently low-risk regardless of symptoms.
Younger patients always have less severe cardiac events.

fields.prompt: What happened when the chatbot was uncertain about a patient's risk level?

fields.text: It asked additional clarifying questions.
It defaulted to the lower-risk category to avoid overwhelming the human queue.
It transferred the patient to a human operator.

fields.prompt: Why did patients who described symptoms as 'tight chest' or 'can't catch my breath' receive lower urgency scores than those who said 'crushing chest pain'?

fields.text: 'Tight chest' is medically less serious than 'crushing chest pain.'

The NLP model was trained on historical descriptions that skewed towards dramatic, clinical language, it penalised informal descriptions rather than treating them as potential flags for atypical presentation.
The chatbot could only recognise medical terminology.

fields.prompt: One patient waited an additional 9 hours after the chatbot said to 'monitor at home.' What does this demonstrate about AI authority?

fields.text: The patient should have ignored the chatbot.
When an AI system endorsed by a health authority tells you to wait, most people will wait, the chatbot's institutional authority actively overrode the patient's own sense that something was wrong.
9 hours is a normal waiting period for non-urgent symptoms.

fields.prompt: The failures were caught during a routine six-month clinical audit. What if the audit hadn't been scheduled?

fields.text: The failures would have been caught by the chatbot's own monitoring.
The pattern of under-triaging would have continued undetected, potentially for years, because the chatbot's real-time monitoring systems did not track clinical outcomes.
Patients would have reported the failures directly.

fields.title: The Triage Trade-Off
fields.description: Test your understanding of this AI failure case study

fields.prompt: The health authority projected a 40% reduction in call waiting times. How does this goal conflict with safe triage?

fields.text: It doesn't, faster triage is always better.
Optimising for speed creates pressure to resolve calls quickly and avoid escalation, the 'lower-risk default' for uncertain cases was a direct consequence of prioritising throughput over safety.
Waiting times are unrelated to triage quality.

fields.prompt: The chatbot agreed with human call handlers 87% of the time. Why is this an insufficient measure of safety?

fields.text: 87% agreement is statistically poor.

Agreement measures how often the chatbot matches human decisions, not whether those decisions are clinically correct. The 13% disagreement may contain the most dangerous cases, and some of the 87% agreement may be cases where both the human and chatbot were wrong.
Human call handlers are always correct.

fields.prompt: Young women experiencing cardiac events often present with atypical symptoms (fatigue, nausea, back pain) rather than 'classic' chest pain. How does this interact with the chatbot's bias?

fields.text: The chatbot handled atypical presentations correctly.

The chatbot's double bias, penalising young age AND penalising non-classic symptom descriptions, created a compounded disadvantage for young women, who are both young and more likely to present atypically.
Atypical presentations are always low-risk.

fields.prompt: If you were redesigning the triage chatbot, what single change would most improve safety?

fields.text: Train the model on more data.
Reverse the default: when confidence is below a threshold, escalate to a human operator, make the system fail-safe (erring towards caution) rather than fail-dangerous (erring towards dismissal).
Add more symptom questions to the conversation.

fields.prompt: Should the chatbot's interface include a way for patients to override its recommendation and escalate themselves?

fields.text: No, patients cannot assess their own medical needs.

Yes, a clear 'I still feel this is urgent' button should always be available, connecting the patient to a human. Patient intuition about their own body is a valid signal that the model cannot capture.
Patients can just call 999 independently.

fields.title: The Hidden Cost of Efficiency
fields.description: Test your understanding of this AI failure case study

fields.prompt: Why did the algorithm deprioritise chronically ill patients?

fields.text: Chronic patients were flagged as 'frequent flyers' and penalised.
Well-managed chronic patients had few recent admissions, which the model interpreted as 'low need' rather than 'good ongoing care.'
The algorithm was designed to prioritise surgical patients.

fields.prompt: Why didn't clinicians simply override the algorithm?

fields.text: The system was legally mandated.
There was no formal override mechanism, and challenging the system was bureaucratically slower than waiting.
Clinicians agreed with the algorithm.

fields.prompt: The model rewarded patients who used hospital services frequently with higher priority. What perverse incentive does this create?

fields.text: Patients will try to get admitted more often.
Patients who successfully manage their conditions outside hospital are penalised, while patients with poor community care are prioritised, the system rewards failure and punishes success.
Hospitals will admit more patients to increase their funding.

fields.prompt: The pattern was noticed by a junior doctor. What does this tell us about who can detect AI failures?

fields.text: Junior doctors are better at data analysis than senior staff.
Frontline clinicians see the real-world impact of algorithmic decisions daily, they are often the first to notice patterns that data teams, working at a distance from patients, miss.
The junior doctor was specifically trained to audit algorithms.

fields.prompt: Three patients escalated to intensive care that staff believed was avoidable with earlier ward admission. What does this represent in terms of system cost?

fields.text: A minor operational issue.

A catastrophic failure of the efficiency optimisation, ICU care costs 3-5 times more than ward care, meaning the algorithm's 'efficiency' in bed allocation may have increased overall costs and patient suffering.
ICU escalation is a normal part of hospital operations.

fields.title: Who Gets the Bed?
fields.description: Test your understanding of this AI failure case study

fields.prompt: Hospital managers praised the algorithm for replacing 'intuition and whiteboard planning' with data. What does this case reveal about the value of clinical intuition?

fields.text: Clinical intuition is always unreliable.

Clinical intuition captures contextual information, why a patient is presenting, how they look, their care history, that admission data alone cannot encode. Replacing it entirely with data loses critical information.
Data is always superior to human judgment.

fields.prompt: The algorithm reduced bed shortages by 18% in its first quarter. Why might this improvement have been misleading?

fields.text: 18% is a small improvement.

The 18% measured operational efficiency (fewer empty beds) but not patient outcomes, the system may have been filling beds with lower-priority patients while higher-priority chronic patients waited in corridors.
The improvement was not statistically significant.

fields.prompt: Chronically ill patients typically present to hospital only when their condition significantly deteriorates. Why does this make the algorithm's behaviour particularly dangerous?

fields.text: Chronic patients are always more expensive to treat.

When a well-managed chronic patient presents to hospital, it usually means something has gone seriously wrong, they are among the highest-acuity patients, not the lowest, and deprioritising them delays critical treatment.
Chronic patients should manage their conditions at home.

fields.prompt: If the algorithm had access to community care data (GP visits, care plans, community nurse records), would it have made better decisions?

fields.text: More data always improves algorithms.

Community care data would have shown that low-admission chronic patients were receiving active, intensive care outside hospital, allowing the model to distinguish 'well-managed serious illness' from 'low clinical need.'
Community data is irrelevant to hospital bed allocation.

fields.prompt: What ethical principle should govern AI-assisted resource allocation in healthcare?

fields.text: Efficiency, minimise waste and empty beds.
Clinical need, resources should be allocated based on the severity and urgency of each patient's condition, with algorithmic recommendations subject to clinical override and regular equity audits.
First-come, first-served, treat patients in the order they arrive.

fields.title: The Self-Fulfilling Map
fields.description: Test your understanding of this AI failure case study

fields.prompt: What is the core mechanism that caused the same neighbourhoods to be flagged as 'high risk' every day for two years?

fields.text: The neighbourhoods genuinely had the highest crime rates in the city.
A feedback loop: more officers led to more arrests, which fed back into the model as evidence of high crime, which sent more officers.
The software had a bug that prevented the map from updating.

fields.prompt: Why was the ten-year arrest dataset a problematic foundation for the model?

fields.text: Ten years of data is too small a sample to be statistically significant.
The data reflected a decade of existing policing priorities and racial disparities, not an objective picture of where crime occurred.
The data was collected before smartphones existed, making it outdated.

fields.prompt: The police department cited a 32% increase in arrests as proof the system was working. Why is this metric misleading?

fields.text: 32% is not a statistically significant increase.
More arrests in targeted zones could simply reflect more policing, not more crime, the system may have been measuring its own enforcement activity.
The arrests were for serious violent crimes that would have happened anyway.

fields.prompt: What monitoring mechanism was missing that could have caught the disparity earlier?

fields.text: A GPS tracker on every officer.
An equity audit that flagged when predictions disproportionately targeted specific racial or socioeconomic groups.
A requirement for officers to file paperwork after every patrol.

fields.prompt: What type of external data could have helped break the feedback loop?

fields.text: Social media posts from residents.
Victimisation surveys, hospital admissions, or anonymous reporting, data that reflects crime experienced, not just crime policed.
CCTV footage analysed by a second AI system.

fields.title: Policing or Predicting?
fields.description: Test your understanding of this AI failure case study

fields.prompt: The heatmap used red, yellow, and green zones. What is the problem with presenting predictions in this format?

fields.text: Colour-blind officers could not read the map.
The traffic-light format implies certainty and urgency, discouraging officers from questioning whether the 'red zone' label is justified.
Green zones might still have some crime.

fields.prompt: Why did the model consistently rate wealthy areas as 'low risk' (green)?

fields.text: Wealthy areas genuinely have zero crime.
Crimes common in wealthy areas (domestic violence, financial fraud) were historically under-reported and under-policed, producing low arrest numbers that the model interpreted as low crime.
The developers intentionally excluded wealthy postcodes.

fields.prompt: What was the real-world impact on residents of neighbourhoods that were constantly flagged as 'high risk'?

fields.text: They received additional community services and investment.
They experienced increased stops, searches, and arrests for minor offences, eroding trust in police and disproportionately affecting daily life.
They were offered the opportunity to relocate to lower-risk areas.

fields.prompt: Who identified the feedback loop and racial disparity in the system?

fields.text: The police department's internal audit team.
An external university research team commissioned by a civil liberties group.
The software vendor during a routine update.

fields.prompt: If you were advising the police department, which reform would most directly address the feedback loop?

fields.text: Upgrade to a more powerful machine learning model.
Incorporate external victimisation survey data and implement mandatory equity audits with automatic pause triggers when racial disparities exceed thresholds.
Increase the number of officers to cover all areas equally.

fields.title: The Hidden Variable
fields.description: Test your understanding of this AI failure case study

fields.prompt: How did postcode function as a discriminatory variable, even though race was not an explicit input?

fields.text: The software had a hidden 'race' field that developers denied.
In a country with deep residential segregation, postcode is strongly correlated with race and poverty, making it a proxy for both.
Postcode data was randomly assigned to defendants.

fields.prompt: Why do people from disadvantaged postcodes statistically reoffend at higher rates?

fields.text: They are inherently more likely to commit crimes.
Systemic factors, lack of jobs, housing instability, fewer rehabilitation services, drive reoffending, not individual character.
They receive shorter sentences that don't act as a deterrent.

fields.prompt: The investigation found that postcode was the single strongest predictor of a high risk score. What does this reveal about the model?

fields.text: Postcode is a scientifically validated measure of criminal tendency.
The model was, in effect, a poverty and geography detector dressed up as a risk assessment tool.
The other features (age, priors, employment) were not included correctly.

fields.prompt: The tool was labelled 'advisory only,' yet judges followed it 84% of the time. Why?

fields.text: Judges were legally required to follow the score.
The precise numeric score created an anchoring effect, a clean, authoritative number that was easier to defer to than narrative judgment, especially under high caseloads.
Judges agreed with the score independently in 84% of cases.

fields.prompt: What test should have been performed before deploying this tool in court?

fields.text: A speed test to ensure scores were generated quickly enough for court schedules.
A disparate impact analysis comparing scores across racial and socioeconomic groups for defendants with identical criminal histories.
A survey asking judges whether they liked the interface design.

fields.title: Justice by Numbers
fields.description: Test your understanding of this AI failure case study

fields.prompt: Marcus, a first-time non-violent offender with a stable job, scored 7/10 ('high risk'). A similar defendant from a wealthy postcode scored 3/10. What does this comparison demonstrate?

fields.text: The model accurately assessed that Marcus posed a higher risk.
The model penalised Marcus for his postcode, not his behaviour, producing a fundamentally unfair outcome.
Marcus had unreported prior offences that the model detected.

fields.prompt: The model was trained on five years of court records. What inherent limitation does this data source have?

fields.text: Five years is not enough data for machine learning.
Court records capture who was caught, charged, and convicted, not who committed crimes. They reflect policing and prosecution patterns as much as criminal behaviour.
Court records are handwritten and difficult to digitise.

fields.prompt: How was the racial disparity in the tool eventually discovered?

fields.text: The tool's developers published an internal audit.
A journalist obtained the scoring data through a freedom-of-information request and published an investigation.
A judge noticed the pattern during sentencing.

fields.prompt: If postcode were simply removed from the model, would that fix the problem?

fields.text: Yes, removing the biased variable eliminates the bias.
Not necessarily, other features like employment status and education level may also correlate with postcode, allowing the model to reconstruct the same pattern indirectly.
Yes, the model would then have no way to estimate risk.

fields.prompt: What is the most important structural change needed when deploying risk tools in criminal justice?

fields.text: Replacing judges with AI entirely for consistency.
Mandatory transparency (publishing the model, its features, and regular disparate impact audits), combined with meaningful judicial discretion to override scores.
Using a more complex deep learning model that is harder to interpret.

fields.title: Drawing the Line
fields.description: Test your understanding of this AI failure case study

fields.prompt: The title references '1930s-style redlining.' What was redlining?

fields.text: A banking term for loans that are overdue.
A historical practice where banks literally drew red lines on maps around minority neighbourhoods and refused to lend there.
A data visualisation technique used in early computing.

fields.prompt: Why did including postcode lead to discriminatory outcomes?

fields.text: Postcodes contain hidden racial data in their format.
In a country with strong residential segregation, postcode correlates heavily with ethnicity, so the model effectively used location as a proxy for race.
The postcode data was entered incorrectly for minority applicants.

fields.prompt: How did the charity prove the system was discriminating?

fields.text: They interviewed rejected applicants about their experiences.
They submitted fictitious paired applications, identical financial profiles from different postcodes, and compared approval rates and interest rates.
They reviewed the model's source code for racial keywords.

fields.prompt: Why did the 2008 financial crisis make the model's postcode bias worse?

fields.text: The crisis caused a computing error in the bank's servers.
Disadvantaged postcodes experienced disproportionately high defaults during the crisis, and the model learned this as a permanent feature of those locations rather than a temporary shock.
The crisis only affected wealthy postcodes.

fields.prompt: The bank's compliance team approved the model. What did they get wrong?

fields.text: They forgot to check whether the model used postcode.
They tested whether protected characteristics were used as inputs, but not whether the model produced equal outcomes for equally qualified applicants across demographics.
They relied on the model's accuracy score alone.

fields.title: Who Gets the Loan?
fields.description: Test your understanding of this AI failure case study

fields.prompt: The charity estimated 4,200 creditworthy applicants were rejected over two years. What is the broader consequence of these rejections?

fields.text: Those applicants simply went to other banks.
Denied access to mainstream credit, many would turn to high-interest lenders or forego purchases, deepening the economic disadvantage the model was already penalising them for.
The rejections had no lasting impact.

fields.prompt: Approved applicants from disadvantaged postcodes were charged 1.8 percentage points more in interest. Why is this a form of discrimination even though they were approved?

fields.text: Higher interest rates reflect genuinely higher risk from those areas.
Equally creditworthy applicants were charged more for the same product based on where they lived, this is a discriminatory pricing penalty, not a risk-based adjustment.
Interest rates are randomly assigned by the system.

fields.prompt: Under UK equality law, this type of discrimination would most likely be classified as:

fields.text: Direct discrimination, the system explicitly used race.
Indirect discrimination, a seemingly neutral criterion (postcode) disproportionately disadvantaged specific racial and ethnic groups.
Not discrimination, postcodes are not a protected characteristic.

fields.prompt: Under the old human-reviewed process, 4,200 of the rejected applicants would have been approved. What does this suggest?

fields.text: Human underwriters were too lenient and approved risky loans.
Human underwriters could evaluate individual circumstances that the algorithm reduced to a postcode score, nuance that was lost in automation.
The old process was slower, so it approved everyone to save time.

fields.prompt: What combination of measures would best prevent this type of failure?

fields.text: Remove postcode and retrain the model.
Remove postcode, conduct disparate impact testing across demographic groups, implement ongoing monitoring of approval and pricing rates by ethnicity and geography, and publish aggregate results.
Replace the model with a newer deep learning system.

fields.title: Lost in Translation
fields.description: Test your understanding of this AI failure case study

fields.prompt: Why did the trading bot interpret the satirical headline as genuine news?

fields.text: The satirical article was designed to deceive AI systems.
The NLP model performed keyword-based sentiment analysis and had no ability to detect tone, genre, or source credibility.
The blog was listed as a trusted financial news source.

fields.prompt: What critical step was missing from the trading bot's pipeline?

fields.text: A step that checked whether the same news was being reported by multiple reputable sources before executing trades.
A step that analysed the stock's 52-week trading range.
A step that consulted human analysts about market direction.

fields.prompt: The bot executed trades within 400 milliseconds. Why was this speed dangerous?

fields.text: Faster trades always generate lower returns.
The speed left no time for any verification, meaning the system acted on unvalidated information.
Human traders could not keep up and felt left out.

fields.prompt: If you were redesigning the system, how would you handle content from unknown or satirical sources?

fields.text: Block all sources that are not on a pre-approved whitelist of reputable outlets.
Weight signals from unknown sources lower and require corroboration from at least two trusted sources before executing trades.
Both A and B are reasonable approaches.

fields.prompt: Why did the initial 8.2% drop in MegaCorp stock spiral into a wider market event?

fields.text: Retail investors panicked and sold everything.
The large sell order triggered automatic stop-losses and algorithmic trades at other funds, creating a cascade where bots were reacting to price movements caused by another bot.
The stock exchange's servers crashed.

fields.title: Market Machine
fields.description: Test your understanding of this AI failure case study

fields.prompt: The bot generated 23% annualised returns in backtesting. Why might this have been misleading?

fields.text: Backtesting used future data (look-ahead bias).
Backtesting uses historical data where satirical articles and novel edge cases may not have appeared, it tests the common case, not the catastrophic one.
23% is not a good return.

fields.prompt: Several retail investors suffered permanent losses even though the market recovered in 12 minutes. How?

fields.text: They were charged a penalty for the crash.
Their automatic stop-loss orders executed at the crash price, selling their holdings at the bottom, and the recovery happened after they had already been sold out.
Their brokerage accounts were frozen during the crash.

fields.prompt: Who should bear responsibility for the losses caused by this flash crash?

fields.text: The satirical blog for publishing the article.
The hedge fund that deployed a system capable of moving markets based on unverified information from any source.
The stock exchange for allowing algorithmic trading.

fields.prompt: What regulatory measure would be most effective at preventing similar incidents?

fields.text: Banning all satirical content about financial markets.
Requiring algorithmic trading systems to include source verification, circuit breakers for unusual single-source signals, and pre-trade risk checks proportional to order size.
Slowing all trades to a minimum of 10 seconds.

fields.prompt: What does this incident reveal about the broader structure of algorithmic financial markets?

fields.text: Markets are too complex for any regulation.

When multiple automated systems react to each other's actions without independent verification, the market becomes a network of interconnected reflexes, fast, efficient, but fragile and vulnerable to a single point of failure.
Algorithmic trading always outperforms human trading.

fields.title: Seeing Through the Rain
fields.description: Test your understanding of this AI failure case study

fields.prompt: Why did the drone misclassify the zebra crossing in rain?

fields.text: The rain physically damaged the drone's cameras.
Fewer than 8% of training images featured wet conditions, the model had rarely seen crossings obscured by water and glare.
Zebra crossings are invisible in rain to all visual systems.

fields.prompt: The model classified the crossing as a 'lane marking' with 54% confidence. What should have happened at this confidence level?

fields.text: The drone should have proceeded but more slowly.
A 54% classification is near-random, the system should have triggered a 'stop and wait' safety behaviour rather than acting on an uncertain result.
54% is sufficient confidence for a safety decision.

fields.prompt: What backup system could have prevented the misclassification?

fields.text: A second, identical camera mounted on the other side of the drone.
A map-based lookup of known crossing locations or LiDAR-based detection of raised kerbs, providing independent confirmation that doesn't depend on visual contrast.
A louder horn to warn pedestrians.

fields.prompt: The drone achieved 98.6% success in dry-weather testing. Why is this figure misleading for a system operating year-round in England?

fields.text: 98.6% is not a high enough number for any autonomous system.
England experiences frequent rain, and if the system wasn't tested extensively in wet conditions, the 98.6% figure only reflects performance in a subset of the conditions it will actually face.
The testing was conducted in a different country.

fields.prompt: A 72-year-old pedestrian was injured. What design principle was most critically violated?

fields.text: The drone should have been painted a brighter colour.
An autonomous system sharing space with vulnerable road users must default to stopping when uncertain, the cost of a false stop is a delayed parcel; the cost of a false proceed is a human injury.
The drone was travelling too fast for a residential area.

fields.title: Sharing the Pavement
fields.description: Test your understanding of this AI failure case study

fields.prompt: How did the pilot expansion from 3 to 12 neighbourhoods contribute to the incident?

fields.text: More neighbourhoods meant the drones had to travel further, draining batteries.
The expansion was based on dry-weather data, scaling a system before testing it in adverse conditions increased the probability of encountering a scenario it couldn't handle.
More neighbourhoods meant more traffic congestion for the drones.

fields.prompt: The injured pedestrian was 72 years old. Why is age relevant to autonomous system safety design?

fields.text: Older pedestrians are easier for cameras to detect.

Older pedestrians may move more slowly, be less able to evade, and suffer more severe injuries from even low-speed impacts, the system must account for the most vulnerable users, not the average user.
Age is not relevant to system design.

fields.prompt: The drone correctly classified the crossing on its outbound journey (dry) but misclassified it on the return (wet). What does this inconsistency demonstrate?

fields.text: The drone's cameras were damaged during the outbound trip.
The model's performance is condition-dependent, it produces correct results in some conditions and incorrect results in others for the same physical location, revealing fragile generalisation.
The crossing's markings deteriorated between the two trips.

fields.prompt: What regulatory requirement would most directly prevent similar incidents?

fields.text: Banning autonomous drones from all public pavements.
Mandating that autonomous systems sharing public space pass safety certification tests that include adverse weather scenarios, with minimum performance thresholds for each condition.
Requiring all drones to be accompanied by a human operator at all times.

fields.prompt: What is the fundamental design principle this incident highlights for autonomous systems in public spaces?

fields.text: Autonomous systems should never operate near people.
When uncertain, the system must default to the action with the least harmful failure mode, stopping (a delayed parcel) rather than proceeding (a potential injury).
The system should always defer to the pedestrian's behaviour.

fields.title: When the Map Lies
fields.description: Test your understanding of this AI failure case study

fields.prompt: What was the root cause of the shuttle freezing at the intersection?

fields.text: A software bug in the shuttle's operating system.
The city repainted road markings, creating a mismatch between the shuttle's pre-built HD map and what its cameras saw, and the system couldn't resolve the conflict.
The traffic lights at the intersection were broken.

fields.prompt: When the shuttle detected a mismatch between its map and its cameras, what did it do?

fields.text: It trusted the camera data and stopped at the new line.
It entered a safety hold, stationary, doors locked, because it could not determine which input to trust.
It reversed and took an alternative route.

fields.prompt: A human driver would have handled this situation easily. What capability does a human have that the shuttle lacked?

fields.text: Better eyesight than the shuttle's cameras.
The ability to reason about why the markings changed, 'they must have repainted the road', and infer that the newer visual evidence should take priority over an older map.
Knowledge of the city council's painting schedule.

fields.prompt: What process failure between organisations contributed to the incident?

fields.text: The university refused to pay the city council for road maintenance.
There was no protocol for the city council to notify the shuttle operator before making road changes, and no process for the operator to receive or integrate such updates.
The shuttle operator did not have a map of the route.

fields.prompt: What would a better fallback behaviour look like when the shuttle detects a map mismatch?

fields.text: Ignore the mismatch and follow the map exactly.
Flag the mismatch to the remote operator, proceed at very low speed to the most conservative stop position (the closer of the two stop lines), and alert passengers that manual oversight is active.
Immediately shut down all systems and evacuate passengers.

fields.title: The Map Is Not the Territory
fields.description: Test your understanding of this AI failure case study

fields.prompt: Passengers were locked inside a stationary shuttle for 22 minutes. What impact does this have beyond the immediate inconvenience?

fields.text: No lasting impact, passengers simply waited.
It erodes public trust in autonomous transport, making passengers feel unsafe and less likely to use the service, potentially undermining adoption of a beneficial technology.
It only affects the university's reputation, not the technology sector.

fields.prompt: How often should HD maps be updated for autonomous vehicles?

fields.text: Once a year is sufficient for most routes.
Continuously, or at minimum whenever road infrastructure changes, with rapid update pipelines and fallback behaviours for the period between a change and the map update.
Only when the vehicle manufacturer releases a software update.

fields.prompt: This shuttle operated on a single 3.5 km route. What happens as autonomous vehicles scale to citywide networks?

fields.text: Larger networks are easier to manage because there are more vehicles.
The probability of encountering a map mismatch increases dramatically, road changes happen constantly across a city, and the map update burden becomes enormous.
Citywide networks don't need HD maps because they can rely on GPS alone.

fields.prompt: The shuttle was designed to trust its map as the primary authority. What alternative design philosophy would be more resilient?

fields.text: Trust only the cameras and ignore the map entirely.

A sensor fusion approach that weighs multiple inputs dynamically, if the map and cameras disagree, the system should reason about which is more likely to be correct based on recency, confidence, and context.
Use a human driver at all times.

fields.prompt: What is the most important operational lesson from this incident?

fields.text: Autonomous vehicles should not operate on public roads.
Deployment of autonomous systems must include formal coordination with all infrastructure stakeholders (road authorities, utilities, construction) and documented protocols for communicating changes.
The shuttle should have been faster so it could clear the intersection before freezing.

fields.title: The Sum of Small Things
fields.description: Test your understanding of this AI failure case study

fields.prompt: Why did the AI classify the system state as 'normal' despite the degrading seal?

fields.text: The sensors were malfunctioning and providing incorrect readings.
Each individual reading was within normal bounds, the danger was in the combination of slight deviations, which had never appeared in the training data.
The AI was not connected to the sensors in the chlorine unit.

fields.prompt: The gas detector showed elevated chlorine but below the alarm threshold. What was wrong with relying on individual thresholds?

fields.text: The threshold was set too high by the manufacturer.
Individual thresholds treat each sensor in isolation, they don't account for the possibility that multiple sensors being simultaneously near their upper bounds is itself a warning sign.
Gas detectors are unreliable for chlorine.

fields.prompt: The AI's confidence dropped to 78% (from its usual 95%+). What should have happened?

fields.text: Nothing, 78% is still a majority.
The drop from 95% to 78% should have triggered an alert to safety officers for a manual check, since a significant confidence drop indicates the system is encountering something unusual.
The system should have automatically shut down the plant.

fields.prompt: The model was trained on four years of data including 14 known incidents. Why was this insufficient?

fields.text: Four years is too short for any machine learning model.
14 labelled incidents is a tiny sample, the model had very few examples of what 'dangerous' looks like, and novel failure modes not represented in those 14 cases would be undetectable.
The data was collected from a different plant.

fields.prompt: The leak was ultimately detected by a human operator who smelled chlorine during a walkthrough. What does this reveal about the role of human inspections alongside AI monitoring?

fields.text: Humans are always better than AI at safety monitoring.
Human senses and judgment detect things that sensors and models cannot, physical walkthroughs provide an independent safety layer that catches novel failure modes the AI was never trained for.
The walkthrough was lucky and cannot be relied upon.

fields.title: Beyond the Dashboard
fields.description: Test your understanding of this AI failure case study

fields.prompt: The AI successfully caught three real issues in 18 months, building confidence. How did this success contribute to the eventual failure?

fields.text: The successes were fabricated by the developers.

Early successes built trust that was then over-generalised, people assumed the AI would catch everything because it had caught three things, reducing vigilance and potentially leading to fewer manual inspections.
The three earlier issues depleted the system's detection capacity.

fields.prompt: The seal degraded slowly over several weeks. Why is gradual degradation particularly difficult for AI monitoring systems?

fields.text: AI systems can only detect sudden changes.

Each day's readings look almost identical to the previous day's, the change is so gradual that it never triggers a step-change alert, and the model continuously recalibrates its sense of 'normal' around the slowly shifting baseline.
Slow degradation doesn't produce sensor data.

fields.prompt: If you were redesigning the system, how would you address the 'novel combination' problem?

fields.text: Add more sensors to increase coverage.

Implement correlation analysis that monitors relationships between sensors, flagging when multiple sensors simultaneously drift towards their upper bounds, even if none individually exceeds its threshold.
Replace the neural network with a simpler rules-based system.

fields.prompt: What broader safety culture issue does this incident highlight?

fields.text: The plant should have hired more safety officers.

The introduction of AI monitoring may have implicitly reduced the perceived need for physical inspections and human vigilance, technology was treated as a replacement for safety culture rather than a supplement to it.
The plant's safety culture was excellent; this was purely a technical failure.

fields.prompt: After this incident, what change to the AI system's logging and alerting would be most impactful?

fields.text: Log confidence scores more frequently.

Create an automatic alert whenever confidence drops below a defined threshold (e.g., below 85% for more than 30 minutes), requiring a mandatory human response, converting passive logging into active escalation.
Send all log data to the AI developer for analysis.

fields.title: The Confident Lie
fields.description: Test your understanding of this AI failure case study

fields.prompt: The chatbot cited a '150 square metres' threshold and a 'two years' condition. Where did these details come from?

fields.text: A national planning guidance document.
Nowhere, they were fabricated by the language model because they sounded like plausible planning conditions.
An older version of the council's bylaws that had been updated.

fields.prompt: Why didn't the RAG system retrieve the correct local restriction?

fields.text: The local bylaws were not digitised.

The national and local documents were stored separately in different formats, and the retrieval step found the national guidance (partially relevant) but missed the local conservation area restrictions (decisive).
The RAG system was not connected to the internet.

fields.prompt: Why did Priya act on the chatbot's advice without further verification?

fields.text: She was trying to avoid paying for professional advice.
The chatbot was hosted on the official council website, giving it institutional authority, and it presented its answer with specific details and no caveats, making it appear reliable.
She knew the advice might be wrong but took the risk.

fields.prompt: What should the chatbot have done differently when answering a planning query?

fields.text: Refused to answer any planning questions.

Included a clear disclaimer that the response was not formal planning advice, cited the source documents it retrieved (or stated that no specific source was found), and directed the user to confirm with a planning officer before taking action.
Asked the user to sign a terms-of-service agreement.

fields.prompt: Planning, legal rights, and financial benefits are all examples of 'consequential queries.' How should chatbots handle these differently from general enquiries?

fields.text: They should provide more detailed answers for consequential queries.
They should actively escalate to a human, providing preliminary information but making clear that formal advice must come from a qualified officer, and offering to book a callback or appointment.
They should charge a fee for consequential queries to indicate seriousness.

fields.title: When the Council Gets It Wrong
fields.description: Test your understanding of this AI failure case study

fields.prompt: Priya spent £28,000 on renovations before discovering the chatbot was wrong. Who bears responsibility for this loss?

fields.text: Priya, for not hiring a solicitor.
The council, for deploying a chatbot on its official website that provided fabricated regulatory advice without adequate safeguards or disclaimers.
The chatbot developer, exclusively.

fields.prompt: The chatbot scored 89% accuracy in pilot testing. Why didn't this catch the planning hallucination problem?

fields.text: 89% is a passing grade and therefore acceptable.

The pilot tested common, straightforward queries, edge cases like queries spanning national and local regulations, which are where hallucinations are most likely, were underrepresented in the test set.
The pilot testing was conducted by the chatbot's own developers.

fields.prompt: The chatbot's answer was partially correct about the national regulation but wrong about local exceptions. Why is partial correctness particularly dangerous?

fields.text: It's not dangerous, getting some of it right is better than getting none right.
Partial correctness is harder to detect than complete nonsense, the accurate parts make the fabricated parts seem credible, and the user has no way to distinguish which parts are real.
Partial correctness only affects experts who would notice the error.

fields.prompt: What is the key difference between using ChatGPT personally and using a council-deployed chatbot?

fields.text: There is no meaningful difference.

A council-deployed chatbot carries the implicit authority of the institution, users reasonably expect that information on an official government website has been verified, creating a higher duty of care.
Council chatbots use better AI models.

fields.prompt: Which combination of measures would most effectively prevent this type of harm?

fields.text: Remove the chatbot entirely.

Add source citations to every answer, display a confidence indicator, include a mandatory disclaimer on consequential topics, implement a 'no source found' fallback that refuses to generate an answer, and offer a one-click escalation to a human planning officer.
Train the model on more planning documents.

fields.title: The Merge Problem
fields.description: Test your understanding of this AI failure case study

fields.prompt: Why did the AI merge two unrelated stories into one false narrative?

fields.text: A developer accidentally linked the two articles in the database.

The stories shared keywords ('Germany,' 'emergency,' 'hospital') and the model's attention mechanism treated keyword overlap as evidence of a relationship, it had no concept of geographic or causal independence.
The AI was programmed to create more dramatic summaries.

fields.prompt: Why did the merged story sound more convincing than the two separate stories?

fields.text: The AI added fictional eyewitness quotes.

A dramatic, causally connected narrative ('explosion forces hospital closure') is more coherent and readable than two mundane, unrelated stories, and the model is optimised to produce coherent text, not truthful text.
The merged story used simpler vocabulary.

fields.prompt: The false summary reached 340,000 readers and caused a 2.3% stock price dip. What amplified the impact?

fields.text: The aggregator paid for social media promotion.
Users shared screenshots on social media without the original source context, stripping away any ability to trace or verify the claim, the falsehood spread faster than the correction.
Traditional news outlets republished the AI summary as their own.

fields.prompt: How was the error eventually caught?

fields.text: The AI's automated fact-checking system flagged it.
A user who had read both original articles separately noticed the summary didn't match either one and reported it.
The editorial team caught it during a scheduled review.

fields.prompt: What design feature would most help users identify merged or fabricated summaries?

fields.text: Making summaries longer so they include more detail.
Linking every claim in the summary to its specific source article, so users can verify that the events described actually appear together in a real report.
Adding a 'trust score' generated by the same AI.

fields.title: Trust but Verify
fields.description: Test your understanding of this AI failure case study

fields.prompt: Editorial spot checks were reduced from daily to monthly as the system appeared reliable. What principle does this violate?

fields.text: The principle that AI systems should never be checked.
The principle that oversight should scale with audience, the system was least supervised precisely when it had the most readers and therefore the most potential for harm.
The principle that monthly checks are always sufficient.

fields.prompt: What automated check could have caught the merged story before publication?

fields.text: Checking whether the summary's word count exceeded a threshold.
Entity resolution and geographic consistency checking, verifying that the locations, dates, and entities in the summary are consistent and actually appear together in the source articles.
Running the summary through a grammar checker.

fields.prompt: 1.4 million users relied on AI briefings as their primary morning news source. What risk does this create?

fields.text: Users read too much news.
If the AI is the only source users consult, there is no independent check on its accuracy, errors propagate unchallenged because users have no baseline to compare against.
Users become too well-informed.

fields.prompt: After the false summary was identified, what should happen to users who already read it?

fields.text: Nothing, they'll probably forget.

The platform should push a prominent correction to all users who received the original summary, clearly explaining what was wrong and why, mirroring the reach of the error with the reach of the correction.
The platform should delete the summary and pretend it never happened.

fields.prompt: Who is responsible when an AI news summary causes real-world harm (stock price drops, public panic)?

fields.text: The AI model itself.
The platform that deployed the AI as a news service, they chose to publish AI-generated content to millions of users and are responsible for the accuracy and safety of what they publish.
The users who shared the false summary on social media.

fields.title: The Phantom Bibliography
fields.description: Test your understanding of this AI failure case study

fields.prompt: How did the AI produce citations for papers that didn't exist?

fields.text: It copied citations from a corrupted database.

It generated citations that were statistically plausible, real author names, real journal titles, believable dates, because it had learned the format of academic references, not because it verified any of them against a real database.
The papers existed but were retracted before publication.

fields.prompt: Some real papers were cited but their findings were described incorrectly. Why is this harder to detect than outright fabrication?

fields.text: Incorrect descriptions are longer and harder to read.
The paper exists and is topically relevant, so a cursory check confirms the citation is 'real', only reading the actual paper reveals that the described findings don't match.
Misrepresentation only affects minor details.

fields.prompt: The two most critical fabricated citations supported the claim that the development would have 'negligible impact' on the wetland. Why is this pattern particularly dangerous?

fields.text: It's a coincidence, the model fabricated citations randomly.
The model generates citations to support the claims it has already written, meaning fabricated references are most likely to appear where the evidence is weakest and the stakes are highest.
The model intentionally fabricated citations to help the developer.

fields.prompt: Why didn't the senior analyst catch the fabricated citations?

fields.text: They were instructed not to check citations.

The citations looked perfectly formatted with real author names and journal titles, the analyst trusted the format and checked the narrative instead, because verifying 34 references would be time-consuming.
The analyst was not qualified to assess the citations.

fields.prompt: What mandatory step should be added to any workflow using AI-generated citations?

fields.text: Ask the AI to double-check its own citations.
Every citation must be verified against an external database (Google Scholar, DOI lookup, library catalogue) before the document is submitted, with the verification documented and auditable.
Limit the number of citations to reduce the chance of fabrication.

fields.title: The Cost of Convenience
fields.description: Test your understanding of this AI failure case study

fields.prompt: The consultancy faced a formal complaint to its professional body. Is this fair, given that a human analyst reviewed the report?

fields.text: No, the AI made the error, not the analyst.
Yes, the consultancy chose to use AI in a professional workflow and remains responsible for the accuracy of documents submitted under its name, regardless of how they were drafted.
Only the AI developer should face consequences.

fields.prompt: The report claimed 'negligible impact' on a wetland SSSI, supported by fabricated citations. What real-world harm could this have caused if the planning officer hadn't checked?

fields.text: No harm, the development would have been fine.
A housing development could have been approved based on false evidence, potentially damaging a protected ecosystem, with the harm only becoming apparent years later when it might be irreversible.
The wetland would have been moved to another location.

fields.prompt: If multiple consultancies adopt the same AI-drafting approach without proper verification, what systemic risk emerges?

fields.text: The consultancies would compete on price.
A widespread pattern of unverified AI-generated reports could systematically weaken environmental protection, approvals based on fabricated evidence would accumulate across hundreds of developments.
Planning authorities would become more efficient.

fields.prompt: The fabrication was caught because one planning officer decided to check citations. What does this reliance on individual diligence reveal?

fields.text: The system works, someone caught it.

A safety mechanism that depends on one person happening to check is not a system, it's luck. Systematic, mandatory verification processes are needed because individual diligence cannot be relied upon at scale.
All planning officers should be required to check every citation.

fields.prompt: What industry-level response would most effectively address the risk of AI-generated citation fabrication in professional reports?

fields.text: Ban all use of AI in environmental consulting.

Establish professional standards requiring documented citation verification for any AI-assisted report, with audit trails showing each reference was checked against an external database, enforced by professional bodies.
Require all reports to use fewer than 10 citations.

fields.title: The Extracurricular Gap
fields.description: Test your understanding of this AI failure case study

fields.prompt: Why did the model score 'Model United Nations' highly but 'part-time work at Tesco' poorly?

fields.text: Model UN develops more valuable skills.

Model UN appeared frequently in profiles of historically admitted students (who were disproportionately from private schools), while part-time work did not, the model learned frequency of occurrence in past successes, not intrinsic value.
The model was programmed to favour specific activities.

fields.prompt: How do extracurricular activities function as a proxy for socioeconomic status?

fields.text: They don't, extracurriculars are equally accessible to all students.

Many high-scoring activities (orchestra, international exchanges, Duke of Edinburgh Gold) require money, equipment, family connections, or schools with extensive programmes, making them proxies for wealth and privilege.
Only sport-related activities are proxies for status.

fields.prompt: A student works 15 hours/week at a supermarket while achieving A*AA grades. Another achieves the same grades with no job and private tutoring. The model scored them identically on academics but the first scored lower overall. What does this reveal?

fields.text: The model correctly identified that employment doesn't improve academic outcomes.
The model cannot assess achievement in context, it doesn't understand that the same grades achieved under harder circumstances represent greater ability and resilience.
Part-time work should be penalised because it takes time from studying.

fields.prompt: The review estimated 320 state school applicants were wrongly rejected or deprioritised over two years. What is the long-term consequence?

fields.text: They applied to other universities and were fine.

Talented students from disadvantaged backgrounds were denied access to an elite institution, perpetuating the cycle of unequal access and reinforcing the data pattern that caused the bias in the first place.
320 is a small number and doesn't indicate a systemic problem.

fields.prompt: This disparity was caught by the university's own equity review. What made this possible?

fields.text: Luck, an individual happened to notice.

The university had a structured internal equity review process that proactively compared outcomes by school type, enabling systematic detection of disparities rather than relying on individual complaints.
Rejected applicants filed a lawsuit.

fields.title: Redefining Merit
fields.description: Test your understanding of this AI failure case study

fields.prompt: The model defined 'merit' based on what past successful students looked like. What is wrong with this definition?

fields.text: Nothing, past success is the best predictor of future success.

Past success at a selective institution reflects who had access, not who had potential. Using it as a template perpetuates existing inequalities and excludes talented people who don't match the historical profile.
The model should have used a longer historical period.

fields.prompt: What data should be incorporated to make the model fairer?

fields.text: Applicants' social media profiles.

Contextual data: school performance relative to national averages, free school meal eligibility, neighbourhood deprivation indices, so the model evaluates achievement relative to opportunity, not in absolute terms.
Parental income, directly.

fields.prompt: Applications scoring below 50 were automatically rejected without human review. Why is this threshold dangerous?

fields.text: 50 is too low, it should be 60.
Automatic rejection removes any possibility of a human recognising context, error, or exceptional circumstances, it makes the algorithm's biases final and unchallengeable.
Automatic rejection is always fair because it applies equally to everyone.

fields.prompt: If the model continues to be used without correction, what happens to the training data over time?

fields.text: The training data naturally becomes more diverse.

The training data becomes increasingly biased, because the model selects private school applicants at higher rates, future successful cohorts contain even more private school students, reinforcing the bias in each training cycle.
The training data remains unchanged.

fields.prompt: What is the fundamental lesson about using AI in high-stakes human decisions like admissions?

fields.text: AI should never be used in admissions.

AI can assist with efficiency, but must be subject to mandatory equity testing, contextual adjustment, and human override for rejected candidates, because 'objective' models inherit the subjectivity of their training data.
AI is always more objective than human reviewers.

fields.title: The Word That Hurt
fields.description: Test your understanding of this AI failure case study

fields.prompt: Why did the model penalise CVs containing the word 'women's'?

fields.text: The developers programmed a rule to penalise gender-specific terms.

In a 78% male training dataset, terms strongly associated with women appeared predominantly on minority-group CVs, the model learned that these terms predicted lower match probability with the dominant (male) pattern.
The word 'women's' is grammatically complex and confused the parser.

fields.prompt: Why did career gaps correlate with lower performance ratings in the training data?

fields.text: People who take career breaks genuinely perform worse.
Managers tended to rate returning employees conservatively in their first review period, the lower ratings reflected managerial bias, not actual capability differences.
Career gaps mean the employee forgot their skills.

fields.prompt: Women's representation in the screening pass-through dropped from 34% to 19%. What does this magnitude of change indicate?

fields.text: Normal statistical fluctuation.
A systematic, algorithmic barrier, a 15 percentage point drop consistent across all role categories cannot be explained by chance and indicates the model is structurally disadvantaging women.
Fewer women applied during this period.

fields.prompt: The training data was 78% male. How does this imbalance affect the model's behaviour?

fields.text: It has no effect, the model evaluates each CV individually.
The model learns that the 'default successful candidate' looks male, male patterns become the template, and deviations from that template (female-associated features) are penalised as anomalies.
It makes the model slightly less accurate for women but still fair overall.

fields.prompt: What preprocessing step would directly address the gendered language problem?

fields.text: Remove all text from CVs and only use numerical data.
Identify and neutralise gendered terms during preprocessing, replacing 'women's football captain' with 'football captain' and removing gender-identifying language before the model scores the CV.
Add more women's CVs to the training data without changing the model.

fields.title: Hiring Fairly
fields.description: Test your understanding of this AI failure case study

fields.prompt: The tool reduced screening time by 75% and was praised as the 'most impactful HR technology investment.' How does this praise create a barrier to addressing bias?

fields.text: It doesn't, efficiency and fairness are unrelated.

When a tool saves significant time and money, there is institutional pressure to keep it running, acknowledging bias means acknowledging that the 'most impactful investment' is causing harm, which creates organisational reluctance to act.
The praise means the tool was working correctly.

fields.prompt: Performance ratings used as training labels contained gender bias. What does this mean for any model trained on those labels?

fields.text: The model will be slightly less accurate but still fair.

The model will reproduce and potentially amplify the bias in the labels, learning that women are lower performers because biased managers rated them that way, not because they actually performed worse.
The model will automatically correct for the bias in the labels.

fields.prompt: The audit focused on gender. What additional dimensions should be tested?

fields.text: No additional testing is needed, gender is the only relevant dimension.
Ethnicity, age, disability, socioeconomic background, and their intersections, a woman of colour with a career gap may be penalised on multiple dimensions simultaneously, with compounding effects.
Only ethnicity, as it's the next most common bias.

fields.prompt: If you were redesigning the system, which approach would be most fundamentally fair?

fields.text: Train the model on a 50/50 gender-balanced dataset.

Combine balanced training data with blind CV processing (removing names, dates, gendered terms), contextual career gap treatment, outcome-based performance measures instead of subjective ratings, and regular disparate impact auditing.
Replace the model with keyword matching.

fields.prompt: What does this case teach about the phrase 'the algorithm is objective'?

fields.text: Algorithms are always more objective than humans.
Algorithms are not objective, they are precise mirrors of the data and decisions they were trained on, including every bias, imbalance, and prejudice embedded in that history.
Algorithms are objective but sometimes make mistakes.

fields.title: The Uniqueness of You
fields.description: Test your understanding of this AI failure case study

fields.prompt: The council said the data was 'fully anonymised' because MAC addresses were hashed. Why was this claim incorrect?

fields.text: The hashing algorithm was weak and could be reversed.
Hashing replaces an identifier with a scrambled version, but it's still a unique, consistent identifier that tracks the same device across all sensors. This is pseudonymisation, not anonymisation.
MAC addresses are not personal data.

fields.prompt: The researcher re-identified 87 people from just their movement patterns. How is this possible?

fields.text: The researcher had access to the council's internal records.
Human movement patterns are highly unique, research shows that just four location-time data points can identify 95% of people. The sensor network collected dozens of points per person per day.
The 87 people had very unusual daily routines.
